candidates.attacker_control: HTTP request parameter names (and values) sent to any handler whose interface-typed parameter is resolved by ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver; createAttribute() passes request.getParameterMap() into MutablePropertyValues, so keys are fully attacker-controlled and flow directly into the SpEL parse at MapDataBinder.java:187.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The snapshot already contains an earlier mitigation: SimpleEvaluationContext.forPropertyAccessors(...) instead of StandardEvaluationContext (lines 180-185), and the changelog lists DATACMNS-1264 'MapDataBinder should reject type expressions in SpEL expressions' (2.0.5, 2018-02-28); this blocks T(...) type references and bean references but is not by itself proof that all method invocation / #this chains, static access or constructor paths are rejected. MapDataBinder is package-private and PropertyTraversingMapAccessor.canRead always true; the changelog stops at 2.0.5 and the pom mixes 1.13.11.BUILD-SNAPSHOT with parent 2.0.10.RELEASE, so the exact commit/fix state could not be pinned down from metadata.
candidates.impact: Server-side evaluation of an attacker-influenced expression inside the application JVM. For this binder class the historical outcome is remote code execution (arbitrary method/class access or command execution under the application's privileges); at minimum unintended object-graph/metadata access and unexpected property writes. Impact is bounded by the restrictions of the evaluation context actually present at runtime (see counterevidence).
candidates.prerequisites: Application enables Spring Data web support (@EnableSpringDataWebSupport / SpringDataWebConfiguration or Spring Boot auto-configuration, which registers ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver for user-defined interface parameter types) or otherwise exposes MapDataBinder through Spring Data web binding; a controller/handler method with such an interface parameter; request parameter names reachable without upstream sanitisation.
candidates.root_cause: MapDataBinder.MapPropertyAccessor.setPropertyValue() parses the raw property name (which originates from HTTP parameter names) with a SpelExpressionParser and evaluates it via expression.setValue(context, value). The only validation, isWritableProperty()/getPropertyPath(), strips all bracket sections with propertyName.replaceAll("\\[.*?\\]", "") before matching the remaining path against the domain type, so arbitrary content inside [...] is validated as harmless yet is still part of the parsed/evaluated SpEL expression; the root object of the evaluation context is the bound map, and PropertyTraversingMapAccessor.canRead() unconditionally returns true.
candidates.title: Attacker-controlled request parameter names are parsed and evaluated as SpEL by MapDataBinder
candidates.trace: request.getParameterMap() -> ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver.createAttribute() (line 161-162) -> new MapDataBinder(type, conversionService).bind(new MutablePropertyValues(request.getParameterMap())) -> DataBinder/AbstractPropertyAccessor -> MapPropertyAccessor.isWritableProperty()/getPropertyPath() strips only [...] content for validation (lines 126-133, 205-209) -> setPropertyValue() parses the full raw propertyName as SpEL (line 187) -> expression.setValue(context, value) (line 190) with map as root object.
candidates.unverified: Whether the spring-expression/spring-beans versions actually used (not present in the snapshot) leave any method-invocation or constructor path reachable through SimpleEvaluationContext on the Java/Spring versions in use; whether a given deployed application actually registers ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver or otherwise routes request parameter names into MapDataBinder; no runtime execution, test, or payload was performed, so exploitability is not confirmed.
candidates.weakness_type: Expression Language Injection (CWE-917) / improper control of code generation leading to potential RCE (CWE-94)

coverage_summary: All 395 readable files listed by get_source_scope fall under src/main (Java library plus resources); get_relation_scope reports 395/395 indexed, no missing files, complete index status, and only static navigation candidates (no SAST or runtime proof). I read the primary trust-boundary code in full — web binding/projection (MapDataBinder, ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver, JsonProjectingMethodInterceptorFactory, ProjectingJackson2HttpMessageConverter, SpringDataWebConfiguration), projection SpEL (SpelAwareProxyProjectionFactory, SpelEvaluatingMethodInterceptor), query SpEL contexts (ExtensionAwareEvaluationContextProvider, DefaultEvaluationContextProvider, SpELContext), and text-searched the tree for SpelExpressionParser, StandardEvaluationContext, Class.forName, getClassLoader, ObjectMapper, and enableDefaultTyping. Mapping/bytecode-generation internals (ClassGeneratingPropertyAccessorFactory, TypeDiscoverer, RepositoryFactorySupport and related) were inspected only at the hotspots surfaced by search, not line-by-line. Dependency jars (spring-expression, spring-beans, Jackson, json-path) are outside the snapshot and were not reviewed.
limitations: Runtime behaviour of the Spring expression context actually used by MapDataBinder could not be verified: spring-expression/spring-beans sources are not in the snapshot, and no execution/tests were permitted.
Exact upstream commit and fix state are uncertain: pom (1.13.11.BUILD-SNAPSHOT, parent 2.0.10.RELEASE) is inconsistent with the changelog, which ends at 2.0.5.RELEASE (2018-02-28).
Reachability depends on application configuration (registration of ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver / Spring Data web support) that lives outside this library snapshot.
No test sources are present, so security-relevant expectations encoded in tests could not be used as corroboration.
Mapping, bytecode-generation, repository-proxy, CDI and config-parsing packages were only screened via search/selected reads, not exhaustively audited.

rejected_leads.lead: ClassGeneratingPropertyAccessorFactory 'Evil' inner class calling ClassLoader.defineClass via reflection
rejected_leads.reason: Matches upstream design (accessor classes are generated in the class loader of the persistent entity type); inputs are mapped entity types, not request data, and there is no path shown from untrusted input to the generated class name/bytecode.
JSONPath expressions come from @JsonPath annotations or method names (developer-controlled), not attacker input; the parsed JSON body is data, not an expression.
Expressions originate from @Value annotations on projection interfaces (developer-controlled); no source evidence in the snapshot that a request selects/creates the expressions.
Evaluation contexts are prepared from declared query methods; method arguments are bound as values, and no sink was traced where attacker input becomes the expression text.
Uses a plain ObjectMapper with FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES=false; no default typing or type-key-driven polymorphic deserialisation observed, and inputs are application-provided repository resources.

rejected_leads.lead: Pageable/Sort handler argument resolvers (unbounded page size / sort parsing)
rejected_leads.reason: Possible resource-consumption hardening gap at most; no source evidence of code execution, injection, or authorisation bypass.

summary: Snapshot is spring-data-commons (395 files, all inside src/main; relation index reports complete coverage). The metadata points to the state just before the 1.13.11/2.0.6 security releases (pom 1.13.11.BUILD-SNAPSHOT; changelog's newest entry is 2.0.5.RELEASE, 2018-02-28, including only DATACMNS-1264 "MapDataBinder should reject type expressions in SpEL expressions"). The strongest source-supported lead is the web property binder: MapDataBinder (reachable from HTTP request parameter names via ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver) validates a bracket-stripped property path but then parses and evaluates the raw attacker-controlled parameter name as a SpEL expression. This is the exact component/root cause class of the spring-data-commons property-binder RCE (CVE-2018-1273); the snapshot contains the earlier, narrower type-expression mitigation (SimpleEvaluationContext) rather than a demonstrably complete restriction on expression evaluation. I could not confirm runtime exploitability (spring-expression is not in the snapshot and code execution is out of scope), so this is submitted as a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
